questions.question: In size reduction, why do we choose m = round(<b1,b2>/<b1,b1>) before updating b2 ← b2 − m·b1?
options: It makes det([b1 b2]) equal to 1, so the lattice becomes unimodular
It minimizes ||b2 − m·b1|| over integer m, keeping the lattice unchanged
It forces b1 and b2 to become orthogonal in one step, like Gram–Schmidt
It guarantees that b2 becomes the unique shortest vector in the lattice
questions.explanation: The squared length ||b2 − m·b1|| is minimized at μ=<b1,b2>/<b1,b1>, so rounding to the nearest integer gives the best lattice-preserving update.

questions.question: Which update is guaranteed to preserve the lattice L(b1,b2) generated by an integer basis (b1,b2)?
options: Replace b2 with b2 − m·b1 for any integer m, preserving the same integer span
Replace b2 with b2/2 when both coordinates are even, shrinking the vectors safely
Replace b2 with its projection onto span(b1), keeping direction but changing length
Replace b2 with coordinate-wise remainders mod b1, keeping numbers small but changing L
questions.explanation: The update b2 ← b2 − m·b1 is a unimodular integer column operation, so it changes the basis but not the integer span.

questions.question: Let b1=(2,1) and b2=(1,7). Compute m=round(<b1,b2>/<b1,b1>) and the updated b2' = b2 − m·b1.
A common Gauss-reduced (2D) stopping condition involves the dot product <b1,b2>. Which inequality matches the 2D criterion?
options: |<b1,b2>| ≤ ||b2||^2, together with ||b1|| ≥ ||b2|| always
|<b1,b2>| = 0, because a reduced basis must be exactly orthogonal
<b1,b2> ≥ 0, because a reduced basis must form an acute angle
questions.explanation: Gauss/Lagrange reduction aims for a short, non-skew basis; the condition 2·|<b1,b2>| ≤ ||b1||^2 captures “small projection” of b2 onto b1.

questions.question: Why does the Gauss/Lagrange algorithm swap b1 and b2 when the updated b2 becomes shorter than b1?
options: To keep the shorter vector first, so the next size reduction uses the best anchor
To avoid changing the determinant, since swapping is the only safe operation
To make the basis orthonormal, since swapping changes angles but not lengths
To ensure the lattice becomes a sublattice of Z^2, which speeds up reduction
questions.explanation: Swapping ensures the next reduction step uses the shortest available vector as b1, which drives progress and matches the reduced-basis ordering.

questions.question: After Gauss/Lagrange reduction in 2D, what does the first basis vector represent (up to sign)?
options: A shortest non-zero lattice vector in L(b1,b2), read off from the reduced basis (up to sign)
The unique closest lattice vector to every target point in R^2, regardless of where the target lies
A generator of the dual lattice whose determinant is minimal among all equivalent dual bases
A short lattice vector with no optimality guarantee, since reduction only approximates SVP in 2D
questions.explanation: In dimension 2, Gauss/Lagrange reduction outputs the successive minima as basis vectors, so b1 is a shortest non-zero lattice vector.

questions.question: Attack intuition: why is “publishing a basis with long vectors makes SVP hard in 2D” false?
options: Because any 2D basis can be reduced quickly to reveal a shortest lattice vector
Because all 2D integer lattices have determinant 1, so density is fixed anyway
Because long basis vectors force the lattice to have no short vectors at all
Because swapping basis vectors changes the lattice point set dramatically
questions.explanation: A basis can hide short vectors, but in 2D Gauss/Lagrange reduction efficiently finds a reduced basis whose first vector is shortest (up to sign).

questions.question: Two different implementations can output different reduced bases for the same 2D lattice. Which statement best explains why?
options: Reduced bases are unique, but implementations often compute determinants incorrectly
Reduced bases are not unique; sign flips and unimodular changes can give variants
Reduced bases are unique only when the input determinant is a prime number
Reduced bases are unique only when the input basis vectors are orthogonal
questions.explanation: Even in 2D, there can be multiple shortest vectors and multiple unimodularly equivalent reduced bases, so outputs can differ while still being correct.
